title: Can identikey-auth keys live IN a secure enclave, or only be enclave-wrapped?
description:
Surfaced 2026-08-01 while explaining ADR-005. Material to what the C3/C4 rungs actually guarantee, and therefore to honest labelling in custody-ladder.md.

TWO SHAPES: (1) key lives IN the enclave - never extractable, enclave signs on request after user verification. Strongest, and what 'enclave-held' implies. (2) key stored encrypted, unwrapped INTO APP MEMORY for use, with only the WRAPPING key in the enclave. Materially weaker: the private key touches memory on every use.

THE CONSTRAINT (BELIEVED, NOT VERIFIED): Apple's Secure Enclave is believed to expose only NIST P-256 through its developer APIs - CryptoKit's SecureEnclave namespace offers only P256.Signing and P256.KeyAgreement, and Security-framework SE keys are limited to 256-bit EC. If so, Ed25519 (and certainly hybrid Ed25519 + ML-DSA per ADR-001's PQ path) CANNOT be enclave-held on Apple hardware - only enclave-wrapped, shape (2).

I COULD NOT CONFIRM THIS FROM PRIMARY SOURCES. Apple's Platform Security guide says only that the PKA supports 'RSA and Elliptic Curve Cryptography' without naming curves; the CryptoKit and Security API pages are JS-rendered and returned no body to a fetch. Note the hardware may support more than the API exposes - the practical constraint is the API surface, not the silicon. VERIFY AGAINST THE ACTUAL API before acting.

ANDROID IS SEPARATE AND MUST NOT BE ASSUMED TO MATCH. Keystore/StrongBox algorithm support differs by API level and by Keymint version; Ed25519 support is newer and may be attestation-only.

DECIDE, ONCE VERIFIED: (a) add P-256 as a cipher suite in identikey-auth for enclave-backed C3/C4 on platforms that require it - identikey-auth is already cipher-agile with a downgrade-proof policy, so this may be cheap; or (b) accept shape (2) and relabel A4 honestly as enclave-WRAPPED, which weakens the rung's claim; or (c) per-platform: held where supported, wrapped where not, with the rung reporting which.

custody-ladder.md now says 'enclave-backed' rather than 'enclave-held' pending this, with the uncertainty flagged inline.
acceptance_criteria: Verified statement of what Apple SE and Android Keystore/StrongBox expose for our algorithms, plus a decision on (a)/(b)/(c) and a corrected A4 description
notes: Correction to the previous note: the identikey-auth implementation issue is ikp-zyq (not ikp-4y6).
close_reason: Answered against Apple primary sources 2026-08-07. Classical: confirmed enclave-WRAPPED only -- SE 'works only with NIST P-256 elliptic curve keys', SecureEnclave.P256 is the sole curve exposed, so Ed25519 can never be enclave-held. Post-quantum: premise partly expired -- SecureEnclave.MLDSA87 supports in-enclave generation and signing as of OS 26.0. Follow-on work split out: identikey-core-zan.7 (custody-ladder labelling) and ikp-zyq (the identikey-auth signer).

title: C2 privilege split: user holds Elect+Transfer, IdentiKey holds Sign+Auth
description:
# av9: C2 privilege split

**Goal.** A C2 identity is one whose XID document assigns Elect+Transfer to a user-held key and Sign+Auth to IdentiKey. A test shows IdentiKey cannot authorize a key-graph change.

## Acceptance
- [ ] ADR-010 written
- [ ] C2 document shows the split; no All
- [ ] authorize_elect rejects our Sign key and accepts the user Elect key
- [ ] C1→C2 transfers inception out and does not retain inception private
- [ ] clippy and cargo-deny clean

## Contract
bc-xid 0.23: Privilege::{Auth,Sign,Elect,Transfer,All,Verify,Update}, Key::add_permission, HasPermissions, XIDDocument::{new,add_key,take_key,remove_key,inception_key}. Mutation does NOT check Elect — we must.

```
XIDDocument::new(XIDInceptionKeyOptions::PublicKeys(pk), XIDGenesisMarkOptions::None)
key.add_permission(Privilege::Elect)
```

## Inherited
- C2 without user-held Elect is C1 (ADR-008 open mechanics).
- bc-xid verifies updates against the inception key by default. If we keep inception private, the split is a promise. After C2 we must not persist it.
- Do not import identikey-storage-auth.

## Out of scope
- C2→C3 ceremony (zan.2)
- Persist documents / pool wiring
- Elect-key wrapping to passkeys (UX)
- Superseding recovery for lost Elect (wzr)
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] ADR-010 settles C1-by-default, Elect provisioning, and Elect loss
- [ ] A C2 document has Elect+Transfer on a user key and Sign+Auth on IdentiKey's, and no key holds All
- [ ] authorize_elect rejects IdentiKey's Sign key (cannot rotate unilaterally)
- [ ] authorize_elect accepts the user's Elect key
- [ ] C1→C2 promotion consumes/forgets inception private and Transfers the inception key out of the document
- [ ] identikey-storage-auth is not involved; clippy -D warnings and cargo deny stay clean
close_reason: ADR-010 decided. C2-native documents assign Elect+Transfer(+Verify+Update) to the user key and Sign+Auth to IdentiKey. authorize_elect rejects our Sign key. C1→C2 Transfers inception out and takes inception private by value. 6 privilege tests plus the existing 22 schema tests. bc-xid does not enforce Elect; we do.

title: TRADEMARK: IDENTIKEY is a registered mark of VASCO/OneSpan in the same category
description:
Found 2026-07-28 while checking domain availability. identikey.com (registered 1998, MarkMonitor - a corporate brand-protection registrar) and identikey.org both redirect to OneSpan's 'Authentication Servers' product page. IDENTIKEY is a registered trademark of VASCO Data Security International (now OneSpan, NASDAQ: OSPN), listed among their marks in SEC filings, for an authentication server product. - ydd.11 proposes a certification mark ('IdentiKey Certified') as the revenue model for the permissive protocol tier. A certification mark in the authentication category is squarely in OneSpan's lane and is exactly the kind of commercial use that draws enforcement. That revenue line may not be buildable on this name.
- ydd.3 (trademark policy as an anti-burial mechanism) presumes we can hold the mark at all.
- Exposure grows as the product becomes visible in enterprise identity - the same market OneSpan sells into.

MITIGATING: OneSpan rebranded IDENTIKEY to 'OneSpan Authentication Server'. A US registration unused for 3 consecutive years is vulnerable to cancellation for abandonment, so the mark may be dormant - a risk AND a possible opening.

ACTION: real trademark search and counsel opinion. USPTO + EUIPO, live status, classes, territories, evidence of continued use. Do this BEFORE further brand investment and before building a revenue line on the mark. This is a flag from a web search, not a legal opinion.

title: Pairwise subject identifiers - decide before the first token is issued
description:
A global self-certifying sub (the XID) lets EVERY relying party correlate the same user across every service they log into. That is a privacy regression versus incumbent IdPs, and an odd look for an identity product built on consent.

OIDC's 'pairwise' subject type exists for exactly this. Likely shape: XID is the canonical internal identity; the sub shown to an ordinary RP is derived from (XID, sector_identifier); the bare XID is disclosed only where the user wants to be linkable (e.g. presenting the same identity to a capability chain or across the sovereign stack).

Painful to retrofit - every issued token embeds a subject that RPs store. Decide before the first token is issued.
notes:
DRAFTED as ADR-009 in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md - 🟡 Proposed, awaiting Duke's call.

THE TRAP THE BEAD DID NOT NAME: stock OIDC pairwise is sub = H(sector || local_id || SERVER-HELD SALT). That makes the OP the only party who can compute or prove the mapping - which reintroduces us as the authority over which subject belongs to which user. ADR-001 explicitly rejects that ('it makes US the authority... precisely the capture the project exists to avoid'). A departing user could not prove to an RP that they are the person it knows, because the linkage lived in our salt. STOCK PAIRWISE FAILS THE EXIT TEST. We cannot just turn on the OIDC feature.

PROPOSED: (1) pairwise by default, bare XID only on explicit per-RP consent; (2) derivation input is USER-HELD material - a dedicated pairwise root committed in the XID document, sub_rp = KDF(pairwise_root, sector) - never a server salt, which is the single constraint that keeps it exit-compliant, since the user can recompute and a successor OP given the same root reproduces every pseudonym exactly; (3) OIDC sector_identifier / sector_identifier_uri; (4) two disclosure modes as a user choice - pairwise RPs canNOT resolve the XID document (ordinary OIDC trust, correct for legacy RPs) while disclosed-mode RPs can (self-certifying, for the sovereign stack) - this resolves the ADR-007 interaction; (5) bind (XID, sector) -> sub_rp on first issuance and refuse a sub_rp already bound to a different XID, else a self-custodial user could assert SOMEONE ELSE'S pseudonym and impersonate them at that RP.

PRIMARY RATIONALE IS ASYMMETRIC REVERSIBILITY, not privacy preference: pairwise -> disclosed is always available later (just another claim); disclosed -> pairwise is impossible (the RP already stored the XID and may already have shared it). One direction reversible, the other a one-way door - default to the reversible one.

KEY CONSEQUENCE: the pairwise root becomes critical material. Losing it costs continuity at EVERY RP simultaneously - a worse blast radius than losing a device key. Must be in the vt4 recovery set on the same footing as keys, and must survive key rotation (so a dedicated secret, not the inception key, since Privilege::Transfer can remove the inception key from the document).

DEFERRED BUT PINNED: at C3/C4 the OP does not hold the pairwise root and cannot compute the pseudonym itself. v1 ships C1/C2 so the mechanism is deferred, BUT the derivation must be pinned now - a pseudonym computed differently later silently breaks every RP account the user already has.

LONG-TERM: a VRF (sub_rp = VRF_sk(sector), proof verifiable against a key in the XID document) gives unlinkability + holder-only computation + OP-verifiability at once, removing the need for the first-issuance binding. Named in the ADR so it is not re-derived later; not adopted for v1.
REVISED 2026-08-01 after Duke's pushback: 'the pairwise root being in the xid, that makes it non-secret... there seem to be a lot of corner cases and dangers in this. is the security tradeoff worth it, especially considering that the oauth auth is not our primary high security auth?'

BOTH POINTS LANDED.

(1) WORDING WAS DANGEROUS. I wrote the pairwise root was 'committed in the XID document'. I meant a hash commitment, but the reading Duke took - the root itself in a publicly-resolved document - would let anyone compute every user's pseudonym at every sector, strictly worse than the bare XID and irreversible once published. On inspection the commitment bought nothing anyway (a hash of the root does not let the OP verify a derivation without the root, and is not needed for recovery or portability), so it is DROPPED rather than clarified.

(2) THE CONSTRUCTION WAS MIS-PROPORTIONED. The OIDC surface is the legacy bridge, not the high-assurance path - that is identikey-auth and the URN grant, whose counterparties are capability-aware and in DISCLOSED mode anyway because capability chains need the real XID. Introducing a new class of critical user-held secret to protect the low-assurance surface bought nothing on the surface that matters.

(3) I ALSO INVENTED THE HARDEST PROBLEM MYSELF. I claimed the OP cannot compute the pseudonym at C3/C4 because it does not hold the root. But the OP mints the OIDC token at EVERY rung - that is the entire purpose of the URN grant. The C3/C4 gap existed only because I insisted the input be user-held. Dropping that removes the gap, the asserted-pseudonym impersonation risk, and the first-issuance binding table together.

(4) AND STOCK PAIRWISE DOES NOT ACTUALLY FAIL THE EXIT TEST - I over-read it. The salt is DATA. Export it and a successor OP reproduces every pseudonym exactly. That is a data-export obligation we already carry and can test, not a cryptographic-architecture obligation. Consistent with the narrowed exit test: it protects the substrate (the XID, which the user controls at every rung), not the feature set. A pairwise sub is a projection for legacy RPs, not the identity.

REVISED DECISION: pairwise by default (the asymmetric-reversibility argument is unchanged and is the real reason), computed by the OP as KDF(salt, XID, sector) with a per-deployment salt that is NEVER published or placed in the XID document, and whose exit obligation is discharged by export. No new user-held secret, no recovery obligation on vt4, no binding table, no VRF for v1.

ACCEPTED: the OP can correlate its own users across sectors. It already can, since it authenticates them. Pairwise defends against RP-to-RP collusion, which is the threat that exists on this surface. A VRF is named in the ADR as the answer IF we ever want the OP itself unable to correlate - but defending the user against US on the legacy OIDC surface is what the URN grant and disclosed mode are for.
DECIDED 2026-08-02. Duke chose to keep pairwise by default, against my revised recommendation to defer it. ADR-009 marked Decided.

MY RECOMMENDATION WAS TO DEFER, and the reasoning is recorded because it bounds the risk if this is ever revisited: pairwise buys PRIVACY, NOT SECURITY (it prevents no attack - not takeover, impersonation, forgery or key compromise - only correlation between RPs); and the one-way-door argument I used to justify it, and which this bead's original 'decide before the first token is issued' framing asserts, is OVERSTATED. The door closes PER RELYING PARTY as each onboards, not globally at first token. Ship a bare XID and add pairwise later and only already-onboarded RPs keep the global identifier. Since the first RPs are the sovereign stack (recrypt, mjolnir, Papyrus) which are capability-aware and want DISCLOSED mode anyway, pairwise protects an RP ecosystem that does not exist yet.

DUKE'S CALL AND ITS MERIT: building it now means never needing the switch at all - no migration, no window where some RPs hold a global identifier and others do not, and no judgement call about which RP is 'third-party enough' to trigger it. The cost is genuinely small: the salt rides on the JWT signing-key infrastructure epic 7 already requires, and the revised construction adds NO per-rung code (the OP computes the pseudonym identically at every rung, since it mints the token at every rung). Reasonable trade.

COMMITTED ACTIONS (now in the ADR): (1) compute sub behind a single seam, never inlined at token construction; (2) subject_type on client registration + subject_types_supported in discovery, pairwise default for new clients, public requires per-RP user consent; (3) salt generated per deployment at install, never a shipped default, stored with JWT signing keys, never logged, included in export, rotation unsupported since it breaks every sub; (4) TEST THE EXPORT PATH - export, not cryptography, is the failure mode that would make this fail the exit test.
RATIONALE CORRECTED 2026-08-02, per Duke: 'Privacy is also a core value, and making identities less correlatable with a minimal extra amount of work is worthy.'

He is right and my framing was wrong twice. I wrote 'privacy, not security' in a way that read as a DEMOTION - as though a privacy control needed some further security justification to earn its place. For this product it IS the point: an identity system built on consent that hands every relying party a global, permanent, cross-service correlation key has conceded the thing it exists to protect, however good its key custody is.

ADR-009 now leads with the privacy rationale as PRIMARY, with the reversibility and no-future-migration arguments explicitly marked as supporting rather than load-bearing. The corrected (weaker) reversibility claim is retained in the ADR so a future reader sees what the decision actually rests on and does not re-inherit the overstated version.
close_reason: Closed

title: AGPL/OpenSSL license conflict: aws-lc-sys 0.36.0 in recrypt-server + recrypt-cli
description:
aws-lc-sys 0.36.0 declares 'ISC AND (Apache-2.0 OR ISC) AND OpenSSL'. The SPDX 'OpenSSL' identifier is the OpenSSL 1.x / SSLeay dual license with the 4-clause advertising clause, which the FSF lists as GPL-incompatible. It is joined with AND, so it cannot be elected around.

Reached from BOTH AGPL binaries via normal (non-dev) edges:
  recrypt-server / recrypt-cli -> recrypt-storage -> aws-config + aws-sdk-s3
    -> aws-smithy-http-client -> rustls -> aws-lc-rs -> aws-lc-sys

AGPLv3 section 7 forbids imposing 'further restrictions'; the advertising clause is one. So the combined work cannot be conveyed under AGPL alone. Commercial licensees are unaffected (no copyleft). The people affected are self-hosters and forkers - i.e. exactly the commons constituency the exit test exists to protect.

VERIFIED FIX: 'cargo update -p aws-lc-rs' resolves 1.15.3 -> 1.17.3 and pulls aws-lc-sys 0.36.0 -> 0.43.0, whose declared license drops OpenSSL entirely (ISC AND (Apache-2.0 OR ISC) AND Apache-2.0 AND MIT AND BSD-3-Clause AND ...). Within semver; dry-run confirms only those 2 packages move. Note aws-lc-sys 0.x releases are semver-incompatible with each other, which is why 'cargo update -p aws-lc-sys' alone reports 0 changes.

CAVEAT: 0.43 changed the DECLARED expression. Confirm against the AWS-LC LICENSE file whether OpenSSL-derived code was removed or the declaration was merely corrected. Automated compliance reads the declaration; counsel reads the file.
close_reason: Fixed: aws-lc-rs 1.15.3->1.17.3 pulls aws-lc-sys 0.43.0 (no OpenSSL). cargo check passes both AGPL binaries; rescan of 659 packages clean. recrypt cdea1c8.

title: Add cargo-deny to CI to keep copyleft out of the commercial tier

A cargo-deny config keeps this true as deps churn; without it the next dependency bump can silently break the ability to sell a commercial exception.

The bead framed this as 'keep copyleft out'; the config draws a sharper line than that - see the note in deny.toml. MPL-2.0 is allowed (file-level copyleft, and webauthn-rs is MPL and mandated by 5gh.1); GPL/AGPL/SSPL are what actually make the commercial half of the dual licence undeliverable. title: Build the C2 -> C3 custody migration ceremony ALONGSIDE C2, not after
description: Managed key handed to the user, server copy destroyed, account keeps working at C3 with the SAME sub. Without this, C2 is rent rather than a service, and it is far harder to add later than to design in. See docs/custody-ladder.md I3.
notes:
ADR-007 ADDS A REQUIREMENT (2026-08-01): the C2->C3 ceremony must relocate RESOLUTION as well as custody. At C1/C2, N=1 (IdentiKey as sole resolver) is fine because we already hold the key. At C3+ the user holds the key, so IdentiKey-as-sole-resolver becomes the only lever we still hold over a self-custodial identity. C3+ therefore requires N>=2 with at least one resolver not operated by IdentiKey. A migration that moves custody but leaves resolution with us is a HALF-MIGRATION - we keep the freshness lever, and per ADR-007 withholding an update is indistinguishable in effect from authorising an attacker. Moving both, or it has not moved custody.
ADR-011 (2026-08-16): do not export managed_key_blob; user Elect authorizes; destroy blob + rung=c3 + N>=2 resolvers in one transaction. Code is nod-c2-c3-exit, not this design activation.

title: Design the Postgres schema: accounts, credentials, custody records, consent log
description:
# zan.1: Design the Postgres schema

**Goal.** identikey-keys owns the durable store everything else sits on: accounts keyed by XID, access credentials, current+historical custody, and the C2 consent log. After this, later beads add behavior on tables that already exist.

## Acceptance
- [ ] sqlx migration creates accounts, credentials, custody_records, custody_events, consent_log, challenges
- [ ] PK is a 32-byte XID (ADR-001), never a pairwise sub or key fingerprint
- [ ] C1/C2 require managed_key_blob; C0/C3/C4 forbid it
- [ ] consent_log is append-only and hash-chained; UPDATE/DELETE fail
- [ ] AAGUID cannot be a policy input
- [ ] identikey-storage-auth is not a dependency
- [ ] tests run against real Postgres; clippy and cargo-deny stay clean

## Contract
sqlx 0.9: `sqlx::migrate!("./migrations")`, `Migrator::run`, `#[sqlx::test]` against real Postgres (ADR-006). XID is SHA-256 of the inception key's CBOR — store as `bytea` length 32.

## Inherited
- `sub` is a XID, not a key fingerprint (LEARNINGS, ADR-001). This bead's original text was stale.
- Do not import identikey-storage-auth (AGPL + recrypt). Take the hash-chain *pattern* only.
- Pairwise `sub` is a token-boundary projection (ADR-009). Never an internal key.
- AAGUID is a UX hint (passkey-requirements R3). Never a CHECK/policy branch.

## Out of scope
- Connection pool / boot wiring (server, still zan.1's sibling comments)
- Store traits / CRUD beyond migration tests
- OIDC clients, refresh tokens, pairwise salt (ccf.*)
- Device records and device_trust claims (zan.8)
- Guardian / SSKR tables (vt4)
- .sqlx offline-cache CI gate (xg2)
- Encrypting managed_key_blob (envelope/KMS is later)
- The C2 Elect-key provisioning ADR (av9)
acceptance_criteria:

title: Read the spec set and write an implementation checklist
description:
# identikey-core-ccf.1: Pin what we implement and refuse before any OIDC endpoint

**Goal.** `docs/oidc-implementation-checklist.md` exists. Later `ccf.4` / `add-oidc-endpoints` cites it. The file names the RFCs we implement, the grants we refuse, and the KDF for pairwise `sub` (ADR-009 left the KDF open).

## Acceptance
- [ ] The file lists **implement** vs **refuse** for: code+PKCE, implicit, ROPC, device code, hybrid, refresh, discovery, JWKS, revoke, introspect, JWT access tokens
- [ ] Refuse-list quotes RFC 9700 (password MUST NOT; implicit SHOULD NOT; PKCE MUST be supported; `S256`; exact redirect match except native localhost port)
- [ ] Pairwise KDF is named (recommendation: HKDF-SHA-256, RFC 5869) so `88b` / `duw` do not invent one
- [ ] `ccf.4` can start without re-reading the RFCs

## Contract
RFC 9700 (Jan 2025), verified https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html:

- §2.1 — AS MUST exact-string-match redirect URIs (exception: native `localhost` port, RFC 8252 §7.3)
- §2.1.1 — AS MUST support PKCE (RFC 7636). If `code_challenge` was sent, MUST enforce `code_verifier`. MUST prevent PKCE downgrade (verifier only accepted if challenge was present). RECOMMENDED: publish `code_challenge_methods_supported`. Clients SHOULD use `S256` (only method that does not expose the verifier)
- §2.1.2 — clients SHOULD NOT use implicit (`response_type=token`) or other types that issue access tokens in the authorization response
- §2.2.2 — refresh tokens for public clients MUST be sender-constrained or rotated
- §2.4 — resource owner password grant MUST NOT be used
- §2.6 — AS MUST NOT allow `http` redirect URIs except native loopback; CORS MUST NOT be enabled on `/authorize`

OIDC Discovery 1.0 issuer: HTTPS URL without query/fragment; `jwks_uri`, `authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint`, `response_types_supported`, `subject_types_supported`, `id_token_signing_alg_values_supported`. ADR-009 adds `subject_types_supported: [pairwise, public]`.

This v1 slice implements: RFC 6749/6750 (code + refresh only), 7636, 8414 + OIDC Discovery, 7009, 7662, 9068 optional, OIDC Core (code). Refuses: implicit, hybrid, ROPC, 8628 device code (not needed to hook an app).

## Inherited
- `sub` is a XID internally; pairwise is a token-boundary projection (ADR-001, ADR-009). Never key tokens on pairwise `sub`.
- Pairwise salt is server-held and exportable; never put in the XID document (ADR-009).
- `identikey-oidc` must not hold user private keys (`crates/identikey-oidc/src/lib.rs`).
- URN grant is A4/`identikey-auth` only, never a WebAuthn assertion (ADR-005) — out of this file’s implement list.
- Do not import `identikey-storage-auth` (AGPL+recrypt). LEARNINGS 2026-07-28.

## Out of scope
- Implementing endpoints — `ccf.4` / `add-oidc-endpoints`
- Salt install / export — `88b`
- The `sub()` function — `duw`
- OIDF suite in CI — `ccf.3` / `nod-oidf-ci` (licence is `nod-oidf-licence`)
- Device-code grant, DCR (RFC 7591), PAR, DPoP — later
- Writing SHALLs into living specs — that is `change` + `fold`
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] docs/oidc-implementation-checklist.md lists implement vs refuse (code+PKCE, implicit, ROPC, device code, hybrid, refresh, discovery, JWKS, revoke, introspect, JWT AT)
- [ ] Refuse-list cites RFC 9700 (password MUST NOT; implicit SHOULD NOT; PKCE MUST; S256; exact redirect match)
- [ ] Pairwise KDF named (HKDF-SHA-256 unless a written reason)
- [ ] ccf.4 can start without re-reading the RFCs

title: ADR-004: RP ID = auth.identikey.me
description: RP ID is effectively permanent; changing it invalidates every enrolled credential and forces full re-enrolment. IdentiKey is an OP serving many RPs across possibly several domains. Decide before the first production credential is written. If multiple origins must share credentials, publish /.well-known/webauthn (Related Origin Requests) from day one - it cannot be retrofitted for already-enrolled users. See docs/passkey-requirements.md R5.
notes:
DRAFTED as ADR-004 - Proposed: RP ID = identikey.io (registrable domain, not a subdomain), plus /.well-known/webauthn from day one. Only missing input is confirmation that identikey.io is the durable production domain. Accepted risk: XSS on ANY *.identikey.io subdomain can exercise the passkey - so marketing/docs/status/user-content must not live under that domain. Standing infra constraint, not a one-time note.
REVISED 2026-07-28 after Duke asked about splitting marketing/app domains. New proposal: dedicated auth origin id.identikey.io IS the RP ID; identikey.io stays marketing; app.identikey.io never does WebAuthn (it redirects to the OP). In an OIDC architecture auth is centralised by construction, so there is structurally only one first-party WebAuthn origin and the usual 'pick the broadest domain' advice does not apply. Also corrects the previous draft's overstated XSS claim: a compromised subdomain can obtain an assertion for a broad RP ID but cannot use it, because clientDataJSON carries the true origin and WEBAUTHN_EXPECTED_ORIGIN allowlists it. Cost of the narrow choice: if we ever need WebAuthn at a second first-party origin, everyone re-enrols. Remaining input: confirm the production domain and pick id. vs auth.
REVISED again 2026-07-28. Duke: 'id.identikey is repetitive, alternative is identikey.me'. Agreed on auth. over id. DNS shows all four of identikey.{io,me,com,org} are held (Cloudflare). Decisive new factor: .io and .me are ccTLDs; .com/.org are gTLDs with no retirement mechanism, and .io has an active sovereignty question post-Chagos. Since the RP ID domain must survive FOREVER and Related Origins does NOT make the RP ID relocatable (it only adds serving origins), put the RP ID on the most durable name owned and serve login from wherever branding wants. Hence auth.identikey.com. identikey.me was genuinely attractive - .me reads as personal identity, and a separate eTLD+1 gives absolute cookie isolation - but it is a ccTLD AND a second permanent renewal dependency.
CORRECTED 2026-07-28: Duke owns only .io and .me - my 'you own all four' was inferred from DNS resolving behind Cloudflare, which proves nothing. .com/.org are OneSpan's. gTLD option gone. Between the two ccTLDs, .me is the more durable: .io has an active post-Chagos sovereignty question, .me (Montenegro) has none. .me also gives absolute cookie isolation from the .io surfaces and reads as personal identity. auth. subdomain rather than the root so a future identikey.me/<handle> profile surface (user-controlled content = XSS surface) stays outside the RP ID permanently.
DECIDED 2026-07-28. Duke confirmed auth.identikey.me. ADR-004 marked Decided in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md. Follow-up operational tasks filed separately (domain lock/auto-renew, /.well-known/webauthn, strict WEBAUTHN_EXPECTED_ORIGIN). Note the scoping: this fixes the credential namespace only, NOT the product name - the trademark question (ydd.12) stays live and the RP ID can outlive a rebrand.

title: ADR-001: sub is a XID (stable identifier from an inception key)
description: The subject of every token, capability and record is the Ed25519 public-key fingerprint, unchanged as a user moves up the custody ladder. Moving C2->C3 changes custody, not identity. This is the invariant that keeps the exit test satisfiable. See docs/custody-ladder.md I1. Blocks any token-format work.

He was right, and it was worse than 'hard': PQ migration is a scheduled rotation, so the original ADR had a known future date on which every identity broke. Now: sub = XID (SHA-256 of the CBOR encoding of the inception signing key), two-tier key model, operational keys rotate underneath. Adopt bc-xid (BCR-2024-010) - XID is already in bc-components 0.31.1 which recrypt depends on, and bc-xid is BSD-2-Clause-Patent, one of the two ADR-003 protocol-tier branches, so it lands in identikey-protocol with zero licence friction. bc-components also ships SSKR (Shamir) for the guardian-recovery epic.

The decision was already made and written up as ADR-001 in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md (commit dd488a8, revised 2026-07-28): sub is a XID, NOT the fingerprint of the current key. The first draft used the current key's fingerprint, which got custody right (C2->C3 keeps the subject) but made key ROTATION change the user's identity. A XID is stable across both custody changes and key changes. See also docs/custody-ladder.md I1. Bead was left open after the ADR landed; no work outstanding.

title: PQClean is being archived - and it is what our ML-DSA runs on
description:
Found 2026-08-07 by the first cargo-deny run on the new Rust workspace. RUSTSEC-2026-0161/0162/0163/0166 mark pqcrypto-mlkem, pqcrypto-traits, pqcrypto-internals and pqcrypto-mldsa unmaintained because upstream PQClean is being ARCHIVED.

PATH: pqcrypto-* <- bc-components 0.31.1 <- bc-envelope <- bc-xid <- identikey-keys / identikey-recovery

WHY THIS IS MORE THAN AN ADVISORY-FEED CHORE:

ADR-001 does not treat post-quantum as speculative. It argues the PQ migration is a SCHEDULED CERTAINTY - it is the reason sub is a XID rather than a key fingerprint, because a fingerprint-based sub would have a known future date on which every identity in the system breaks. The whole two-tier key model exists to make that migration survivable.

So the ML-DSA implementation is not incidental infrastructure. It is the thing a load-bearing architectural decision was made in anticipation of, and it is now unmaintained beneath us. Being archived is worse than being merely stale: no security fixes are coming, for the algorithm we intend to migrate the entire identity system onto.

Not urgent - we perform no ML-DSA operations today, and identikey-auth's hybrid support is where this actually lands. But it must be answered BEFORE the migration, not during it, and the answer is a supply-chain question rather than a code change.

ACTION: identify the maintained successor for ML-DSA/ML-KEM in Rust (aws-lc-rs, RustCrypto's ml-dsa, or whatever the ecosystem consolidates on); ask Blockchain Commons what bc-components intends, since they face the same problem and their answer probably decides ours; remove or re-justify the deny.toml ignores once there is a plan. Coordinate with the identikey-protocol repo - identikey-auth owns the hybrid signing surface.
acceptance_criteria: A named, maintained source for ML-DSA is identified and the migration path off pqcrypto-* is written down; the deny.toml ignores are removed or re-justified against it

title: RUSTSEC-2023-0071: bc-xid drags in the vulnerable rsa crate (Marvin timing attack)
description:
Found 2026-08-07 while wiring cargo-deny into the new Rust workspace. NOT filed by a human reading an advisory feed - filed because the very first cargo-deny run failed, which is the tool working.

PATH: rsa 0.9.10 <- ssh-key 0.6.7 <- bc-components 0.31.1 <- bc-envelope <- bc-xid 0.23.0 <- identikey-keys

RUSTSEC-2023-0071 is a non-constant-time RSA implementation leaking private key bits through network-observable timing. There is NO patched version - the advisory states 'No safe upgrade is available'.

WHY IT IS CURRENTLY IGNORED (documented in deny.toml): IdentiKey performs no RSA operations at all. Signing is Ed25519 with hybrid ML-DSA. RSA is present only because bc-components pulls ssh-key for SSH key format support. No RSA private-key operation means no timing oracle.

WHY THIS IS STILL A BEAD RATHER THAN A CLOSED QUESTION:

1. This is a consequence of ADR-001 (adopt bc-xid) that the ADR did not record. The dependency is a permanent tenant of our graph as long as bc-xid is, and we accepted it without noticing.
2. THE IGNORE IS CONDITIONAL AND THE CONDITION IS EASY TO BREAK. If we ever accept an SSH RSA key - as a resolver credential, a guardian key, or an import format - dead code becomes a live signing path and the ignore silently becomes a real vulnerability. Guardian recovery (vt4) is exactly the kind of feature that might reach for SSH key formats.
3. It is a supply-chain question worth raising with Blockchain Commons: does bc-components need ssh-key's RSA support at all, or can it be feature-gated off? A default-features=false path upstream would remove this for every downstream user, not just us.

ACTION: raise upstream with Blockchain Commons; check whether feature flags can drop ssh-key or its RSA support; re-check at the point any SSH key handling is proposed. Point identikey-core-ydd.13 (external security review) at this too.
acceptance_criteria: Either the rsa crate leaves the dependency graph, or the ignore in deny.toml is re-justified against a current threat model; either way the answer is written down, not assumed

title: JWKS signing key rotation - and the salt that must NOT rotate beside it
description:
Migrated from sprint-status.yaml 13.1 (TS/Keycloak era). Operational rotation of the OP's JWT signing keys: publish the new key in JWKS before signing with it, honour an overlap window of at least the max token lifetime, then retire.

DISTINCT FROM XID KEY ROTATION. This is the OP's own service keys, not a user identity rotation (ADR-008). Do not let the two share a mental model or a code path.

CRITICAL INTERACTION WITH identikey-core-88b: the pairwise salt is stored alongside these signing keys, and it must NEVER be rotated - rotating it breaks every pairwise sub at every relying party simultaneously. A key-rotation runbook or automation that treats 'rotate the material in the signing key store' as one operation is a catastrophic outage waiting to happen. The runbook must call this out and the salt must be structurally excluded from any rotation tooling.
acceptance_criteria: New key published in JWKS ahead of use; overlap window honoured; old key retired only after max token lifetime; runbook states explicitly that the pairwise salt is co-located but NOT rotated
notes: 2026-08-19 realign: pairwise salt non-rotation is done (88b, PairwiseSalt, never rotated). SigningKey generate/load/persist exists (add-oidc-endpoints). Remaining is JWKS overlap rotation: publish new key before signing, honour max token lifetime, retire old. Do not share a path with XID key rotation or salt.

title: Refresh token lifecycle: hashed storage, rotation, revocation checked on every use

Store SHA-256 hashes, never raw tokens, linked to user and device with expiry and revocation status. Rotate the refresh token on use. Check revocation on refresh AND on introspection - an endpoint that verifies only the signature will happily accept a revoked token, which is the whole failure mode this exists to prevent.

title: Label C3/C4 honestly: the hybrid is enclave-WRAPPED on the classical half
description:
Consumer half of identikey-core-46v, now answered. custody-ladder.md's C3/C4 rungs must say which shape is actually in force, because the two are materially different guarantees and 'enclave-held' implies the stronger one.

Verified against Apple primary sources (CryptoKit DocC JSON): the Secure Enclave 'works only with NIST P-256 elliptic curve keys' and SecureEnclave.P256 is the only curve exposed, so ADR-001's Ed25519 half is enclave-WRAPPED -- the seed is unwrapped into app memory on every signature -- and can never be otherwise on Apple hardware. But as of OS 26.0 SecureEnclave.MLDSA87 supports in-enclave generation and signing, so the PQ half CAN be enclave-held; identikey-auth does not do that yet (ikp-zyq).

So a rung label has to carry three states, not two: enclave-held, enclave-wrapped, and mixed -- and the mix depends on OS version and on whether ikp-zyq has landed.
acceptance_criteria: custody-ladder.md distinguishes enclave-held from enclave-wrapped explicitly and states which applies per key half; the claim is tied to a runtime capability probe (SecureEnclave.isAvailable and OS floor), not asserted statically; ADR-001's PQ path notes that the PQ half is the one that can be hardware-resident.
notes: 2026-08-19 act wave: claimed for parallel implement
close_reason: custody-ladder.md and ADR-001 distinguish enclave-held vs wrapped vs mixed per key half; probe lives in native client (5571da6).

title: Test the pairwise export path - it is the exit-test obligation
description:
ADR-009 action (4). Pairwise passes the exit test only because the salt is EXPORTABLE: a successor OP given the same salt reproduces every pseudonym exactly, so a departing user keeps continuity at every relying party. That makes export - not cryptography - the failure mode here. An untested export path is how this decision silently becomes capture.

Test the whole round trip: export a user's data, load it into a separate deployment, and confirm the reissued tokens carry identical sub values for the same sectors.
acceptance_criteria: An automated test exports and reimports into a second deployment and asserts identical sub values per sector

The one thing that makes that retrofit expensive is defining a rotation ceremony or event format with nowhere to carry a next-key digest - that turns a clean retrofit into a format break across every identity.

bc-xid preserves unrecognised assertions during parsing, so carrying the commitment as an extension assertion should be nearly free. CONFIRM THIS before shipping rather than during the hardening pass: check that the rotation ceremony, the event/envelope format, and any signature coverage we define leave room for an additional assertion without a version bump.

title: Verify the committed successor digest during C2->C3 migration

The user's device must verify that the digest published in the XID document matches the key it generated locally, BEFORE treating the migration as complete. Without this check the migration hands the identity over at exactly the moment it is supposed to hand it back.

title: Threshold resolver reads with fail-closed duplicity detection (ADR-007)
description: ADR-007 (4): query K of N declared resolvers, order by bc-xid provenance mark, take the highest. Two VALID documents not on the same provenance chain is a duplicity signal - FAIL CLOSED, do not pick a winner. Freshness tiers: ordinary OIDC login may use a cached document within a short TTL; key-graph changes, delegation issuance, custody migration and wallet-class actions require a fresh threshold read. C1/C2 default N=1; C3+ requires N>=2 with at least one resolver not operated by IdentiKey, K=2.
acceptance_criteria: Duplicity (two valid docs, divergent provenance chains) fails closed with a test; consequential operations cannot be served from cache

title: Serve the XID document as a convenience resolver, with a short TTL and revocation signal
description: ADR-007 (5): the OP serves the XID document over a well-known path as an AVAILABILITY service holding no authority the document does not grant it. Needs a short TTL plus a push/revocation signal - the worst case is an RP honouring a rotated-out compromised key for the length of its cache. Staleness is a security property, not an availability inconvenience: serving an old validly-signed document after a compromise rotation presents the attacker's key as current.
acceptance_criteria: Well-known endpoint serves the signed document; TTL is short and documented; a rotation triggers a revocation signal rather than waiting out the cache
close_reason: GET /.well-known/xid/{xid} serves stored bytes; 60s must-revalidate + SHA-256 ETag. b5f71e8

title: Resolver relocation as a first-class self-service ceremony (ADR-007)
description: ADR-007: the XID document declares its own resolvers via bc-xid resolution_methods(). Because the set is signed, relocation must be a document update the user can perform themselves, not a support request. If relocation is not self-service, the exit test degrades from 'leave intact' to 'leave and hope someone cached you'. Rotating the resolver set is itself a key-graph change and must require the same authority as Privilege::Update - otherwise the resolver set becomes the soft underbelly of the identity.
acceptance_criteria: A user can add, replace and remove resolvers without IdentiKey's cooperation; resolver-set changes require Update authority and are provenance-marked
notes: ADR-011: first resolver relocation is the C2→C3 ceremony. Later relocation is the same Elect/Update write without a rung change.

title: XID document resolution: who serves it, how does an RP get fresh key state?
description:
The real remaining cost of ADR-001. A stable identifier is only useful if a relying party can obtain current key state. Candidates: the OP, a user-controlled endpoint, recrypt storage, or a witness set.

Smaller than it looks: because the XID document is SIGNED BY THE SUBJECT, a resolver can serve it but cannot forge it. Losing our resolver costs freshness, not verifiability - an availability dependency, not a trust dependency. But a user must be able to self-host or relocate resolution, or the exit test degrades from 'leave intact' to 'leave and hope someone cached you'.
notes:
DRAFTED as ADR-007 in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md - status 🟡 Proposed, awaiting Duke's call.

CORRECTS THIS BEAD'S PREMISE. The bead reasoned that because the XID document is subject-signed, a resolver can serve but not forge it, so losing our resolver costs 'freshness, not verifiability - an availability dependency, not a trust dependency.' That is not quite right. A resolver can serve an OLD, VALIDLY-SIGNED document. If K1 is compromised and the user rotates to K2, the prior document is still correctly signed and still lists K1 - so a stale serve presents an attacker's key as current. Withholding an update is indistinguishable in effect from authorising the attacker. Staleness IS a security property; resolution is partly a trust dependency.

PROPOSED: (1) the document declares its own resolvers via bc-xid resolution_methods() - signed, so relocation is a document update not a support request; (2) bc-xid Provenance marks are the ordering primitive, so 'newer' is verifiable without trusting the server; (3) threshold reads - query K of N resolvers, take the highest mark, and FAIL CLOSED on two valid documents not on the same chain (duplicity); (4) freshness tiers - cached within TTL for ordinary OIDC login, fresh threshold read for key-graph changes, delegation issuance, custody migration, wallet-class actions; (5) the OP is a convenience resolver, never a root of trust.

KERI: adopt the witness PATTERN, decline the stack. CESR/ACDC vs our dCBOR/Gordian substrate would mean a permanent translation layer between two canonical encodings. Rust KERI crates are fragmented and thin (keri 28k, keri-core 20k, keriox 1.5k, keri-rs 285 'under active development') vs bc-xid 38k and BSD-2-Clause-Patent, which is already ADR-003's protocol-tier licence.

VERIFIED against bc-xid 0.23.0: Privilege has 14 variants including Auth, Sign, Issue, Delegate, Elect (rotate keys), Update (service endpoints), Transfer, Revoke. XIDDocument has resolution_methods(), delegates()/add_delegate()/find_delegate_by_xid(), provenance(), to_signed_envelope() with XIDVerifySignature::Inception.

OPEN IN THE ADR: values of K and N, and whether N=1 (IdentiKey only) is acceptable for C1/C2 users who have not designated their own resolvers.
DECIDED 2026-08-01. Duke approved the threshold-resolver design and the canonical-format stance. ADR-007 marked Decided in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

K/N RESOLVED, and the ladder decides it: at C1/C2, N=1 (IdentiKey alone) is an acceptable default, because at those rungs IdentiKey ALREADY HOLDS THE KEY - a dishonest custodian need not lie about resolution, it can simply sign, so resolver honesty is dominated by custodian honesty and extra resolvers buy nothing. At C3/C4 the calculus inverts: the user holds the key, so IdentiKey-as-sole-resolver would be the only remaining lever we hold over a self-custodial identity - exactly what the exit test exists to remove. So C3+ requires N>=2 with at least one resolver NOT operated by IdentiKey, K=2 for the consequential tier.

CONSEQUENCE FOR zan.2: resolver relocation is now part of the C2->C3 migration ceremony. Climbing to self-custody without relocating resolution is a half-migration that leaves us holding the freshness lever.
close_reason: Closed

title: Trademark + certification mark policy (anti-burial AND the revenue model for the permissive tier)

Serves two purposes at once, which is why it should be prioritised above its apparent importance.

REVENUE: the protocol tier is Apache-2.0 OR BSD-2-Clause-Patent, so embedding it is free and generates no license revenue - by design. For a permissively-licensed protocol the monetizable asset is the MARK, not the copyright. 'IdentiKey Certified' licensed on passing the conformance vectors. title: Design guardian selection UX
description: The hardest unsolved problem on the ladder, and the one that determines whether anyone actually reaches C3.

title: Review the guardian-key-recovery and threshold-crypto prior art for what is reusable
identikey-recovery - the floor that makes everything else safe
description: Load-bearing: the decision not to nag users about multiple passkeys (R2) is only correct if recovery works. Guardian quorum, Shamir, MPC ceremony. Prior art in ~/work/IdentiKey/{guardian-key-recovery,threshold-crypto,key-recovery-py}.
notes:
ADR-008 ADDS AN OBLIGATION (2026-08-01): pre-rotation is adopted, so each rotation commits to the digest of the next key set in advance. This creates a NEW WAY TO LOSE AN IDENTITY - losing the pre-committed successor material while still holding a valid current key. The C3 recovery design (guardian quorum / Shamir / MPC) must therefore cover successor material exactly as it covers the current key. If recovery restores the current key but not the committed successor, the identity is recoverable but no longer rotatable, which is a slow-motion loss.
SCOPED DOWN 2026-08-01 (correcting my note of the same day). ADR-008 was revised: pre-rotation is now REQUIRED at C3/C4 and OPTIONAL at C0/C1, not universal - with a single custodian holding both current and successor there is no security benefit at all. So the successor-recovery obligation I added applies only WHERE PRE-ROTATION IS ON, i.e. C3/C4 and whoever holds Elect at C2. Not a blanket requirement across all rungs.

The obligation itself stands for those rungs: losing pre-committed successor material costs rotatability while the current key still works. And note the harder half, filed separately: any recovery path from lost successor material is also an attack path (KERI's 'superseding recovery'). That must be solved before C3 ships.
COUPLED TO zan.5 (2026-08-01). ADR-008's C3 synthesis: the guardian quorum is the natural custodian for pre-rotation successor material. Guardian-held successor shares put it in a security domain distinct from the hot key (earning the full pre-rotation guarantee) AND make it recoverable (removing the soft-identity-loss risk of a lost successor). This makes vt4 a prerequisite for pre-rotation at C3, and gives the guardian design a second job to account for beyond current-key recovery.
THIRD OBLIGATION (2026-08-01, ADR-009): the PAIRWISE ROOT must be in the recovery set alongside key material. Losing it costs the ability to prove continuity at EVERY relying party simultaneously - a wider blast radius than losing a device key, because the user does not lose one login, they lose the linkage to every account they ever created. It must also survive key rotation, which argues for a dedicated secret rather than deriving from the inception key (Privilege::Transfer can remove the inception key from the XID document). Recovery design now covers: current key, pre-rotation successor (where enabled), and pairwise root.
RETRACTING the third obligation I added earlier today. ADR-009 was revised: the pairwise derivation now uses an EXPORTABLE SERVER-HELD SALT, not user-held material. So the pairwise root does NOT enter the recovery design. vt4 stays scoped to key material: current key, plus pre-rotation successor where enabled (zan.5, itself deferred from v1 and optional). The salt is our operational secret to protect and export, not a burden placed on the user or on guardian recovery.

title: ADR: can a WebAuthn assertion satisfy the challenge-response URN grant?
description: Does urn:identikey:params:oauth:grant-type:challenge-response accept a WebAuthn assertion, or strictly a raw Ed25519/P-256 signature? Determines whether custody rungs C1/C2 (via passkey) and C3/C4 (via enclave key) share one verification path or two. Affects the shape of identikey-oidc and the protocol spec. See docs/passkey-requirements.md open question 4.
notes:
DRAFTED as ADR-005 - Proposed: NO. The URN grant accepts only an identikey-auth Response; WebAuthn goes through the ordinary auth-code flow. They prove different things (hold the key vs hold a passkey registered to an account) with different replay models. Accepting both at the token endpoint means two parsers, two replay defences and two downgrade surfaces on the most security-critical path. Ladder framing: WebAuthn is A3 authenticating you TO the party holding your key; the URN grant is A4 where you hold it. Different row and column.
DRAFTED as ADR-005 in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md (commit 9d1e1d8) - status 🟡 Proposed, awaiting Duke's call. Proposed answer: NO. The URN grant accepts ONLY an identikey-auth Response; WebAuthn authenticates through the ordinary authorization-code flow. Rationale: the two prove different things - the URN grant proves 'I hold the IdentiKey key' (raw signature over domain-separated canonical dCBOR, verifier-issued nonce, audience-bound), while a WebAuthn assertion proves 'I control an enrolled authenticator'. Unifying them behind one verifier would muddle the custody ladder's rungs. Bead stays OPEN because the ADR is Proposed, not Decided - this is a real pending decision, not bookkeeping drift.
DECIDED 2026-08-01. Duke: '005 seems good.' ADR-005 marked Decided in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

ANSWER: NO. The URN grant accepts only an identikey-auth Response. WebAuthn authenticates through the ordinary authorization-code flow.

ORIGINAL RATIONALE: the two prove different propositions - the URN grant proves 'I hold the IdentiKey key' (raw signature over domain-separated canonical dCBOR, verifier-issued nonce, audience-bound), a WebAuthn assertion proves 'I hold a passkey registered against an account'. Accepting both at the token-minting endpoint means two parsers, two replay defences and two downgrade surfaces, for convenience the auth-code flow already provides. Ladder framing: WebAuthn is A3 (authenticates you TO the party holding your key), the URN grant is A4 (you hold the key yourself) - different column and different row.

TWO STRONGER ARGUMENTS ADDED ON LANDING, both postdating the draft:

(1) PRIVILEGE SEPARATION WOULD BE DEFEATED AT THE TOKEN BOUNDARY. ADR-008 splits bc-xid privileges so at C2 the user's key holds Elect+Transfer and ours holds Sign+Auth. A passkey is a credential holding AUTH. The key satisfying the URN grant may hold Sign, Elect, Transfer. If a WebAuthn assertion satisfied the grant, an Auth-only credential would mint tokens indistinguishable from ones backed by full key authority - collapsing the separation at the one place it most needs to hold.

(2) IT MAKES I2 STRUCTURALLY ENFORCEABLE RATHER THAN POLICY. A passkey is re-registerable via an A1 mechanism (email link). If a passkey assertion satisfied the URN grant, an email link would TRANSITIVELY REACH A C3 KEY - the exact silent collapse to C1 that I2 calls a release blocker. Refusing the assertion at the grant makes that unreachable by construction.

CONSEQUENCE BULLET CORRECTED (2026-08-01) after Duke asked why a passkey is needed at all if you hold the key locally: a C3/C4 user reaches their key through LOCAL USER VERIFICATION, which on a native app is the platform biometric over an enclave/keychain item and involves NO passkey. WebAuthn appears at C3/C4 only in a browser via the prf extension, as key-wrapping rather than authentication. See custody-ladder.md 'Local user verification is not an access level'.
close_reason: Closed

title: Two crypto backends: openssl and rustls are both linked - decide whether that stands
description:
Found 2026-08-07 when the scaffold's deny.toml banned openssl and the ban failed immediately. The ban was written on an unchecked assumption that rustls was the only backend; it is not, and the ban would have forbidden a crate our own decisions mandate.

  openssl <- josekit                     (JOSE / token signing)
  openssl <- webauthn-attestation-ca <- webauthn-rs   (mandated by 5gh.1)
  rustls  <- sqlx, the HTTP stack        (TLS termination)

The webauthn-rs path is not negotiable without abandoning the maintained Rust WebAuthn implementation, which is not a serious option. josekit IS negotiable - it was picked in ccf.4 for JOSE and there are rustls/RustCrypto-native alternatives.

THE COST OF LEAVING IT: two vulnerability feeds to watch, two crypto implementations to reason about in any audit (ydd.13), a native openssl build in every container and CI image, and a more complicated story if FIPS or a formal review ever comes up. None of that is fatal, and plenty of production auth servers link both. But it should be a decision on the record rather than an accident of dependency selection.

Cheapest real reduction is replacing josekit. Worth checking what it would cost before ccf.4 builds on it, because after that the switch is a refactor rather than a choice.
acceptance_criteria: Either the graph is reduced to one crypto backend, or the two-backend position is recorded as deliberate with its operational cost stated

title: External security review before the first production users
description:
Migrated from sprint-status.yaml 13.2 (TS/Keycloak era), where it was a generic 'security audit & penetration testing' line. It is worth more than that here.

The specific things an external reviewer should be pointed at, because they are novel rather than standard-web-app risk:
- The C2 privilege split (av9) - does IdentiKey genuinely lack Elect, or does some admin path route around it?
- The URN grant (ccf.5) - ADR-005 made it the only key-authenticated path to tokens; it is now a single high-value target.
- Threshold resolver reads and duplicity detection (5f3) - fail-closed under a hostile resolver.
- The A1/key-recovery boundary (vt4.1) - I2 is a release blocker if breached.
- Pairwise salt handling (88b) - leakage deanonymises every user across every RP at once.

Timing: this must happen before real users hold C2 keys, because after that the blast radius of a finding includes other people's identities, not just our schedule.
acceptance_criteria: External review commissioned and its findings triaged onto the board before any real user holds a C2 key

title: A1 bootstrap and account recovery: email magic link and SMS OTP
description:
Migrated from sprint-status.yaml 13.3-13.6 (TS/Keycloak era). Email magic link and SMS OTP as bootstrap (enrol a credential) and as ACCOUNT recovery. Apple/Google social re-verification recovery is the third member of this set; the bootstrap half of social is already covered by identikey-core-ccf.6.

THE INVARIANT THIS LIVES UNDER: custody-ladder I2. These are access level A1 - account recovery ONLY, never key recovery, and available at C1/C2 only. If an email link can ever reach a key, the email provider becomes the real root of trust and the entire ladder silently collapses to C1. identikey-core-vt4.1 is the enforcement bead; this is the feature that makes it necessary. Build them together, not in sequence.
acceptance_criteria: Email/SMS can bootstrap an account and enrol a credential; a test proves no A1 path can reach key material at C3+; the account/key boundary is asserted in code, not just documented

title: Superseding recovery: lost successor material without opening an attack path
description: ADR-008 consequence, deferred but must be solved BEFORE C3 ships. Where pre-rotation is on, losing the pre-committed successor costs ROTATABILITY - the identity is still usable with the current key but can never be rotated. Any recovery path from that state is, by construction, also a path an attacker could use to override a legitimate pre-rotation commitment. This is KERI's 'superseding recovery' problem; they resolve it with multi-sig thresholds and witness-ordered event precedence. Audit their treatment before designing ours.
acceptance_criteria: A documented recovery path from lost successor material, with an argument for why it is not usable by an attacker holding the current key
notes: COUPLED TO zan.5 (2026-08-01). ADR-008 now makes superseding recovery a PREREQUISITE for enabling pre-rotation at C3, not a later refinement: without it, lost successor material means the identity can never be rotated again, with no escape. Pre-rotation and this bead move together — both deferred from v1, both required before C3 ships. Do not enable pre-rotation at C3 until this exists.

title: Pre-rotation: optional, gated on successor separation (ADR-008) - deferred from v1
description: Largely superseded by ADR-001's move to XID - XID's rotation model covers successor keys. The remaining piece is PRE-ROTATION: KERI commits to a digest of the next key at each rotation, so a compromised current key cannot rotate to an attacker's key. Matters most at C3/C4 where there is no custodian to appeal to. Determine whether bc-xid supports it and whether we need it, BEFORE the protocol split lands.
notes:
VERIFIED 2026-08-01 against bc-xid 0.23.0 (crates.io/docs.rs). The crate has: Privilege enum (14 variants: All, Auth, Sign, Encrypt, Elide, Issue, Access, Delegate, Verify, Update, Transfer, Elect, Burn, Revoke), Permissions struct, Key struct, Delegate struct, Service struct, Provenance struct, XIDDocument with resolution_methods(), delegates(), provenance()/next_provenance_mark_with_embedded_generator(), to_signed_envelope(), and XIDInceptionKeyOptions.

NOT YET CONFIRMED: explicit PRE-ROTATION (a commitment to the digest of the NEXT key set). Provenance marks give a verifiable chain of revisions, which is adjacent but not the same guarantee - provenance proves this revision follows that one; pre-rotation proves a compromised CURRENT key cannot rotate to an attacker's key, because the successor was committed in advance. Docs describe bc-xid as 'an early implementation' and 'not yet feature complete', so absence from the docs is not proof of absence. Needs a source-level check of bc-xid-rust before the protocol split.

RECOMMENDATION (see ADR-007): adopt pre-rotation regardless of whether bc-xid ships it - it is a hash commitment, cheap, and pulls in none of the KERI stack. If bc-xid lacks it, carry it as an extension assertion on the XID document rather than forking the crate.
RESCOPED 2026-08-01. This is no longer 'evaluate whether' - ADR-008 decided YES, adopt pre-rotation. What remains is implementation.

ORDER OF WORK: (1) source-level check of bc-xid-rust for a native next-key digest commitment - docs.rs shows Provenance (chained revisions) but that is a WEAKER guarantee: provenance proves this revision follows that one; pre-rotation proves a compromised CURRENT key cannot rotate to an attacker's key because the successor was fixed in advance. bc-xid self-describes as 'early implementation, not yet feature complete', so absence from docs is not proof of absence. (2) If absent, carry the commitment as an EXTENSION ASSERTION on the XID document - bc-xid preserves unrecognised assertions during parsing - rather than forking the crate.

RAISED TO P0: ADR-008 requires pre-rotation to exist BEFORE the first production key is inceptioned. It cannot be retrofitted onto identities that never committed a successor digest. This now gates key inception, not just the protocol split.

NEW OBLIGATION ON vt4: losing the pre-committed successor becomes a way to lose the identity while still holding a valid current key. Successor material must be covered by the C3 recovery design exactly as the current key is.
REVISED 2026-08-01 after Duke's objection. TWO CORRECTIONS TO MY EARLIER NOTE:

(1) LOWERED BACK TO P1. I raised this to P0 claiming pre-rotation 'cannot be retrofitted onto identities that never committed a successor digest'. That was WRONG. Any rotation may begin committing a successor; what cannot be recovered is protection for rotations that already happened uncommitted. Starting late is safe provided the key is not already compromised (a breached current key can commit the attacker's own successor). Committing from inception is better, but it is not a one-way door, so it does not gate first inception.

(2) SCOPED BY RUNG, NOT UNIVERSAL. Duke: 'pre-rotation implies a custodian - so it must be optional if we're to onboard fully managed keys; and with a full custodian that's also holding the pre-rotated next key, it obviates any security benefit.' Correct. Pre-rotation is hot/cold separation WITHIN ONE CONTROLLER. Benefit is proportional to separation between where current and successor live: same party same domain = NONE; same party colder domain (offline HSM, separate KMS) = partial; different parties = full. So: REQUIRED at C3/C4, OPTIONAL at C0/C1 (cosmetic - a fully managed user has nowhere separate to keep a successor), and at C2 it applies to whoever holds Elect.

THE REAL MECHANISM for non-rent managed custody is PRIVILEGE SEPARATION, not pre-rotation - see ADR-008 Decision 3. bc-xid's Elect ('add or remove other verifiers') and Transfer are distinct from Sign/Auth and separately assignable. At C2: IdentiKey holds Sign+Auth, USER holds Elect+Transfer. Breach of IdentiKey yields Sign not Elect (no permanent theft); exit is unilateral (user rotates us out without our cooperation). Orthogonal tools: pre-rotation defends one holder against hot-key theft, privilege separation defends the user against their custodian.
DEFERRED FROM v1 — 2026-08-01. Duke: ship without pre-rotation, add it in a hardening pass. Agreed, and ADR-008 revised again.

DUKE CAUGHT A CONTRADICTION IN MY ADR: it published a table saying 'same party, same security domain = NO benefit' and then mandated pre-rotation at C3/C4. But a C3 user with a SINGLE DEVICE is same-party-same-domain — successor in the same enclave, behind the same unlock, exposed to the same compromise. For that user pre-rotation is STRICTLY NEGATIVE: no protection gained, plus a new way to lose the identity. Duke's framing: 'soft identity loss where they can never do another rotation.'

The loss mode is asymmetric and worth stating precisely: losing the committed successor does not break the identity today (current key still signs), it removes the ability to EVER ROTATE AGAIN. Identity frozen to one key forever; when that key is eventually lost, aged out or compromised there is nothing to move to. A slow fuse on an identifier whose premise is lifetime stability.

REVISED RULE: the condition is SEPARATION, NOT RUNG. Off by default at every rung including C3/C4. On only when the successor lives in a custody domain distinct from the hot key (second device, hardware token, offline HSM, guardian shares). NEVER on with the successor in the same domain — the software should refuse that configuration rather than offer it. Not a naked toggle: the user chooses to establish separate successor custody, and pre-rotation follows from that, so nobody enables the loss risk without first creating the thing that earns the benefit.

C3 SYNTHESIS: guardians should hold the successor. At C3 a guardian quorum already exists; generating the successor into guardian-held shares puts it in a genuinely distinct domain (full guarantee) AND makes it recoverable (kills the loss risk). Resolves both sides at once — but couples pre-rotation to vt4 (guardians) and wzr (superseding recovery). PRE-ROTATION AT C3 CANNOT SHIP AHEAD OF THOSE.

GATE (replacing 'a hardening pass'): must exist before the first C3/C4 identity does, not before v1. Introduced at the C2->C3 migration rotation, which generates a fresh user-held key we never possessed — so the late-adoption hazard (a compromised current key committing the attacker's own successor) does not reach that population. Extension point tracked as 29v.

title: ADR: Postgres access layer - sqlx vs tokio-postgres; pglite scope
description: Standardising on Postgres. Leaning sqlx with the offline query cache checked in (compile-time-checked SQL is worth the build friction in an auth server). Also decide pglite's scope: recommended only for genuine in-process embedding (desktop app), NOT as the dev default - divergence shows up exactly where it hurts (concurrency, advisory locks, SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on token/challenge tables).
notes:
DRAFTED as ADR-006 - Proposed: sqlx with the offline query cache committed; real Postgres in dev and CI; pglite only for genuine in-process embedding (desktop app), never the dev default.
DRAFTED as ADR-006 in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md (commit 9d1e1d8) - status 🟡 Proposed, awaiting Duke's call. Proposed answer: sqlx with the offline query cache committed; real Postgres in dev and CI; pglite reserved for genuine in-process embedding (desktop app), never the dev default. Rationale: compile-time-checked SQL is worth the build friction in an auth server, where a wrong query is a security bug rather than a 500; and a pglite/Postgres dev-prod split diverges exactly where it hurts (concurrency, advisory locks, SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on the challenge and token tables). Consequences: DATABASE_URL needed at build time unless the offline cache is current, so CI must verify the cache is not stale; recrypt-server's direct tokio_rusqlite use needs converting (tracked as zan.4). Bead stays OPEN - Proposed, not Decided.
DECIDED 2026-07-30. Duke: 'yes, as suggested.' ADR-006 marked Decided in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md: sqlx with the offline query cache committed; real Postgres in dev and CI; pglite reserved for genuine in-process embedding (desktop app), never the dev default. Added four committed actions to the ADR: (1) commit .sqlx/ plus a CI staleness check, (2) real Postgres service container in CI with no SQLite/pglite fallback in the test path, (3) convert recrypt-server's direct tokio_rusqlite usage via the store traits (zan.4), (4) if pglite lands for desktop it runs the same migrations and trait impls, with its divergences tested explicitly. Filed the CI staleness gate as a separate bead since it is the one that makes the compile-time checking real.
